Chapter 3: The Systems That Shape How We See Ourselves
Most of us grow up thinking our struggles with body image are personal—maybe even our fault. But, what if I told you there’s so much more at play than just individual choices or so-called flaws?
The truth is, the way we value—or sometimes devalue—bodies is shaped by powerful systems that touch every part of our lives. These systems decide who gets to feel safe, who gets called beautiful, and even who’s allowed to take up space.
Imagine someone who uses a wheelchair. Every single day, they’re faced with buildings that just weren’t built for them, stares from strangers, or comments that reduce them to nothing more than their disability. The real problem isn’t their body—it’s a world that refuses to make room for difference.
And it’s not just about disability. The same thing happens for people of color, for transgender folks, for anyone whose body doesn’t fit into that narrow box of what’s considered “normal.”
These are systems—like racism, sexism, ableism—that work together to create a kind of hierarchy. Some bodies are celebrated, while others are ignored, or even punished. And this isn’t just some distant idea; it shows up in our laws, in the stories we see on TV, and in everyday moments—like how doctors treat their patients, or who gets labeled “healthy” or “attractive.”
For lots of people, these systems are invisible. They move through the world without ever stopping to think, “Why are certain bodies always favored?” But if you’re on the outside looking in, the message rings loud and clear: you don’t belong.
And that exclusion? It’s not just hurtful—it’s actually dangerous. It can mean worse health outcomes, fewer chances at opportunities, and a constant sense of being under threat.
There are moments when the pressure from these systems can feel overwhelming. Maybe someone’s denied a job because of how they look, or gets harassed just for being themselves in public. These aren’t just one-off stories—they’re part of a bigger pattern that keeps certain bodies down, while protecting others.
But here’s the good news: there’s hope. When we start to notice how these systems work, we can begin to challenge them. And that takes more than just changing ourselves—it calls for us to come together. To speak up when we see injustice, support those on the margins, and create spaces where everyone feels welcome.
Of course, this isn’t easy. It means facing some hard truths, letting go of privilege, and being willing to make mistakes along the way. But it matters. The world won’t change unless we’re willing to see where it’s broken—and to imagine something better.
Radical self-love is one of our most powerful tools in this fight. It gives us the strength to push back against those messages that say we’re not enough. It helps us find beauty in our differences, and to demand justice for every body.
When we join together with this kind of courage and compassion, we start to break down the barriers that keep us apart.
The journey’s not short, and there will be challenges. But every act of resistance, every moment of kindness, brings us a little closer to real equality.
That’s the promise of radical self-love: it’s not just about healing ourselves—it’s about freeing all of us, together.
